'''John C. Holden''' (born 1934), often called '''Jack Holden''', is an American [[geologist]], [[Technical illustration|scientific illustrator]], and [[humorist]] known for his early research into [[Tectonics|tectonic drift]] with [[Robert S. Dietz]] in the 1960s and 1970s.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Ruch |first=John |last2= |first2= |last3= |first3= |date=2020-05-31 |title=From his rustic cabin, 85-year-old geologist and artist Jack Holden has his offbeat off-the-grid lifestyle down to a science |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/pacific-nw-magazine/from-his-rustic-cabin-85-year-old-geologist-and-artist-jack-holden-has-his-offbeat-off-the-grid-lifestyle-down-to-a-science/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |website=The Seattle Times |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1976 he founded the "International Society to Stop Continental Drift", a tongue-in-cheek organization which attracted hundreds of members and had the motto, "Eschew Sea-Floor Spreading".

== Early life ==
Holden was born in 1934 in [[Colón, Panama]], and was raised in [[San Diego]] by his mother and her husband Warren Holden, a Navy officer.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=About |url=http://johncholden.com/about.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150224230355/http://johncholden.com/about.html |archive-date=2015-02-24 |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=johncholden.com}}</ref> Holden's biological father was a San Diego [[Milk delivery|milkman]] named Bud. As a child in the 1940s, Holden explored the canyons of California for days at a time and hunted rabbits with a [[Pellet (air gun)|pellet gun]].<ref name=":0" /> When he played [[blackjack]] and [[acey-deucey]] with friends, he was known to bring a paper with the pre-calculated winning odds.<ref name=":0" />

Holden disliked schoolwork and preferred to draw cartoons in his notebook. Due to his learning difficulties, he was enrolled in specialized program from the [[San Diego State University]]'s teacher college.<ref name=":0" /> In sixth grade, he developed an art style called "psychodoodles" during class.<ref name=":0" /> Holden eventually graduated from high school at age 21, and was accepted into San Diego State University, where he studied geology, earning a master's degree in 1961.<ref name=":0" />

== Geology research career ==
[[File:Collected reprints - Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratories (and) Pacific Oceanographic Laboratories (1968) (20665481095).jpg|thumb|Holden's illustration of a continental terrace wedge published by the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] in 1968]]
In 1961, Holden was hired by the [[Navy Electronics Laboratory|Naval Electronics Laboratory]] geologist [[Robert S. Dietz]], a prominent researcher in the new and controversial fields of [[plate tectonics]] and [[impact crater]]s.<ref name=":0" /> For more than 10 years, Holden served as Dietz' illustrator and collaborator, adding creative elements and scientific diagrams in many of Dietz' journal articles, for which Holden was named co-author.<ref name=":0" /> Dietz and Holden were early "drifters", advocates for the theory that Earth was covered by slowly drifting tectonic plates.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1965-03-11 |title=The 'Man in the Moon' Dead For at Least 3 Billion Years |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kansas-city-star-the-man-in-the-moo/199209548/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=The Kansas City Star |pages=13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=1971-02-10 |title=Some doubt reality of Continental Drift |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-shreveport-journal-some-doubt-realit/199209017/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=The Shreveport Journal |pages=9}}</ref> They theorized that the [[Moon]]'s surface was static, and that its craters were 3 billion-year-old remnants of astroid collisions.

The decade-long collaboration between Dietz and Holden involved stints in [[Washington, D.C.]] and [[Miami]]. During this period, Holden studied in a [[paleontology]] PhD program at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] but failed to graduate despite finishing his [[Thesis|dissertation]] because he could not meet the requirement to read technical [[German language|German]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> In 1973, Holden lost his job with Dietz due to budget cuts.<ref name=":0" />

== Independent endeavors and publications ==
Holden later said that in the 1970s, "I more or less reconciled myself to being a dropout" and "decided to try to make it on my own."<ref name=":0" /> He continued to publish his illustrations and science writing,<ref>{{Cite news |date=1971-06-19 |title=How The Continents Have Drifted |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/tucson-citizen-how-the-continents-have-d/199209356/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=Tucson Citizen |pages=38}}</ref> and began selling products including his "psychodoodle" drawings and custom [[globe]]s with moveable continents that he had developed for [[Robert S. Dietz|Dietz]].<ref name=":0" /> He founded (and later sold) Softwear Unlimited, which sold graphic [[t-shirt|tees]] with science jokes, such as an illustration of [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]] as a traffic police enforcing the [[speed of light]]: "186,000 miles per second is not only a good idea. It's the law."<ref name=":0" />

In 1973, he began working with [[William R. Corliss]] to compile the multivolume "Catalog of Anomalies", which contained unusual or unexplained results from old scientific publications.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Ruch |first=John |date=2019-09-23 |title=He saw the scientific promise in the paranormal, but now his legacy could be lost |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/magazine/he-saw-the-scientific-promise-in-the-paranormal-but-now-his-legacy-could-be-lost/2019/09/23/e42c02e6-c8e8-11e9-a4f3-c081a126de70_story.html |access-date=2026-06-10 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Corliss |first=William |date=2002 |title=A Search for Anomolies |url=http://www.scientificexploration.org/jse/articles/pdf/16.3_corliss.pdf |journal=Journal of Scientific Exploration |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=439–453 |archive-date=September 27, 2006 |access-date=June 10, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060927083817/http://www.scientificexploration.org/jse/articles/pdf/16.3_corliss.pdf |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref> The books were praised by the journal [[Science (journal)|''Science'']], and the science fiction author [[Arthur C. Clarke]] was a fan of them.<ref name=":0" />

Holden collaborated with Dietz again on their self-published 1987 book, ''Creation/Evolution Satiricon: Creationism Bashed'', a takedown of religion.<ref name=":0" /> He has illustrated work by Peter Vogt,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Peter |first=Vogt |date=March 2023 |title=John/Jack Holden Cartoons |url=https://www.calvertmarinemuseum.com/DocumentCenter/View/4470/Ecphora-March-2023?bidId= |journal=The Ecphora}}</ref> poetry books by the oceanographer Harris B. Stewart Jr.<ref name=":2" />

== Humor ==

=== ''Journal of Irreproducible Results'' ===
Holden contributed humor writing to the ''[[Journal of Irreproducible Results]].'' Editor [[Norman Sperling]] later called Holden the publication's "most memorable" writer.<ref name=":0" />

=== International Stop Continental Drift Society ===
In 1976, Holden founded a satirical club called the "International Stop Continental Drift Society" which aimed to put an end to [[seafloor spreading]], [[Volcano|volcanic]] activity, and [[earthquake]]s greater than 4.0 on the [[Richter scale]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=International Stop Continental Drift Society {{!}} UIA Yearbook Profile {{!}} Union of International Associations |url=https://uia.org/s/or/en/1100005093 |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=uia.org}}</ref> He jokingly told ''[[Newsweek]]'' that "something had to be done" because China and California would converge and cause "[[Chinese Communist Party|Communists]] to marry our children".<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=1983-06-26 |title=Scientific satirist says "Stop Continental Drift" |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-mobile-register-scientific-satirist/199202788/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=The Mobile Register |pages=99}}</ref> He promoted a tongue-in-cheek counter-theory called "[[continental drip]]", based on the observation that continents appear to drip down toward the [[South Pole]].<ref name=":1" />

Members paid $5 annual dues for a society newsletter published sporadically, "like natural disasters", that featured humor, research, and cartoons (such as a drawing of a whooshing continent rapidly approaching, captioned "Look Out! Here Comes Africa").<ref>{{Cite web |title=International Stop Continental Drift Society (ISCDS) Newsletters and epehemra by Holden, John C. (Society President): (1978) {{!}} Carpe Diem Fine Books, ABAA |url=https://www.abebooks.com/International-Stop-Continental-Drift-Society-ISCDS/32335574951/bd |access-date=2026-06-09 |website=www.abebooks.com |language=en}}</ref> Society headquarters was the house in [[Winthrop, Washington|Winthrop]] where Holden lived with his elderly mother,<ref name=":1" /> and it was included in the ''[[Encyclopedia of Associations]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1986-10-02 |title=How does one qualify for the Banana Club? |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-edwardsville-intelligencer-how-does/199210610/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=The Edwardsville Intelligencer |pages=4}}</ref> Bumper stickers for the group had the slogan "Stop Continental Drift", as well as "Reunite [[Gondwana]]land" and "Join the Mothers' March Against Volcanos".<ref name=":1" /> [[Arthur A. Meyerhoff]], prominent tectonic theory researcher, displayed the sticker on his car.<ref name=":1" />

By the mid-1980s, the Society had grown to 700 members,<ref>{{Cite news |date=1984-12-13 |title=Laughter ferments the scientific culture |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-oregonian-laughter-ferments-the-scie/199209038/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=The Oregonian |pages=89}}</ref> including both supporters of tectonic theory and a sect of opponents, which Holden estimated at 10% to 20% of the group.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1981-10-02 |title=Club out to stop continental drift |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/corvallis-gazette-times-club-out-to-stop/199203166/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=Corvallis Gazette-Times |pages=16}}</ref><ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=1981-09-15 |title=One More Worry: The Threat of Continental Drift (Or Is It 'Continental Drip'? |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/kitsap-sun-one-more-worry-the-threat-of/199212296/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |work=Kitsap Sun |pages=5}}</ref> Members from the geology department of [[Leiden University]] held a humorous event on campus to "bolt down" the [[Eurasian plate]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=International Stop Continental Drift Society |url=http://www.weirduniverse.net/blog/comments/international_stop_continental_drift_society |access-date=2026-06-09 |website=Weird Universe |language=en}}</ref> For the 40th anniversary of the prank in 2018, the university brought Holden and his wife to campus, where Holden presented an unconventional pet theory that continental drift was not caused by [[heat current]]s but by the spin of Earth.<ref name=":0" />

=== Other humorous endeavors ===
Holden also founded the "Manzana Institute of Geotechnic Redundancies"<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Illustrated Dictionary of Physics |url=https://dsimanek.vialattea.net/illusdic.htm |access-date=2026-06-10 |website=dsimanek.vialattea.net}}</ref> and the "Friends of the Okanogan Lobe" (FOOLs), a group of retirees that makes local expeditions to study [[Glaciology|glacial geology]].<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Holden was unmarried for much of his career, and "didn't want to be sucked into a system where you have a demanding [[wife]] and a bunch of [[Child|kids]]" that [[Child penalties|limit career options]].<ref name=":0" /> In 1973 he bought a house with his brother in [[Kirkland, Washington|Kirkland]], before later moving deeper into the woods, in [[Winthrop, Washington|Winthrop]], with his elderly mother.<ref name=":0"/> When he moved her into a nursing home in 1989, he met his future wife Linda, who worked there. Linda later said, "It was his [[Intellect|brain]] I fell in love with".<ref name=":0" />

In 1990 the couple moved to an octagonal, [[Off-the-grid|off-the-grid home]] within the [[Colville Indian Reservation]] in [[Okanogan County, Washington]].<ref name=":0" /> The home uses [[solar power]], [[Well|well water]], and a [[Wood-burning stove|wood stove]] for heat, and he installed a [[gas generator]] so that Linda can watch television.<ref name=":0" /> They have about seven [[cat]]s. A neighbor lives in an [[Observatory|astronomical observatory]] that Holden built on the property.<ref name=":0" />

=== Personality and hobbies ===
Though he lacks an official diagnosis, Holden describes himself as being [[Dyslexia|dyslexic]] and [[Autism|autistic]].<ref name=":0" /> For more than 28 years, Holden has maintained a daily record of [[weather]] and other information on illustrated paper [[scroll]]s, which are more than 82 feet long.<ref name=":0" /> He collects animal [[skeleton]]s, [[gun]]s, [[Rock (geology)|rocks]], and other items.<ref name=":0" />

Holden has long held [[anti-establishment]] beliefs, and told ''[[The Seattle Times]]'' that "what life is all about, as far as I'm concerned, is having [[fun]]."<ref name=":0" /> He criticizes politicians for their perceived lack of care for skepticism and the [[scientific method]], and has questioned certain aspects of [[climate change]].<ref name=":0" /> Writing in ''The Seattle Times'', John Ruch called him "one of those unique [[wikt:maverick|mavericks]] that the [[Western United States|American West]] is so good at producing."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ruch |first=John Ruch |date=2020-05-31 |title=How the 'Handbook of Unusual Natural Phenomena' led to a unique human specimen in Okanogan County |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/pacific-nw-magazine/how-the-handbook-of-unusual-natural-phenomena-led-to-a-unique-human-specimen-in-okanogan-county/ |access-date=2026-06-09 |website=The Seattle Times |language=en-US}}</ref>
